Overview

Nicosia as a Business Centre

Nicosia (Lefkosia) is the capital of the Republic of Cyprus and the island's main administrative and commercial centre. The government, the Central Bank of Cyprus, the Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission (CySEC) and the national courts of appeal are based in the city, alongside the headquarters of Cypriot banks, law and audit firms, and the corporate service providers that administer many of the island's international holding companies. Financial services contributed about 10 percent of Cypriot gross value added in 2024 and professional services about 7 percent. Nicosia is also Europe's last divided capital: the UN buffer zone runs through the old city, and the northern part is administered by the Turkish Cypriot authorities, recognised only by Turkey.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Nicosia because ownership, financing and professional services for companies active far beyond Cyprus are frequently arranged there. Typical triggers include due diligence on Cypriot holding companies and their directors ahead of acquisitions or financing; research on investment firms, fund managers and payment businesses supervised by CySEC or the Central Bank; tracing assets and nominee relationships for creditors and litigants using Cypriot freezing and disclosure remedies; and background work on advocates, trustees and fiduciaries involved in a structure. Matters touching the northern part of the city raise distinct questions, because records, courts and registries there sit outside the Republic's legal system and are not recognised by the EU.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Nicosia

01

Cypriot holding company due diligence

Research on holding and financing companies administered from Nicosia, covering registered directors, secretaries and filed accounts, links to corporate service providers, nominee arrangements and the ultimate owners behind them, to support acquisitions, lending, joint ventures and onboarding decisions involving Cypriot structures.

02

Investment firm and fund counterparty research

Background on CySEC-supervised investment firms, forex and CFD brokers, fund managers and their key persons, drawing on public registers, published regulatory decisions and settlements, court records and media, for clients assessing distribution, outsourcing, partnership or investment relationships.

03

Asset tracing for Cypriot proceedings

Fact development supporting Cypriot advocates who seek freezing, disclosure or Norwich Pharmacal relief in the Nicosia courts, mapping companies, directors, property interests and transaction chains so counsel can frame applications aimed at banks, service providers and related parties.

04

Fiduciary and professional intermediary checks

Lawful background research on trustees, administrators, advocates and accountants involved in a structure, including disciplinary history, litigation and adverse media, where a client needs to understand who controls documents, signatures and bank mandates for a Nicosia-administered company.

05

Northern Nicosia counterparty exposure

Risk research on businesses and individuals operating in the Turkish Cypriot-administered north, where records sit outside the Republic's registries and courts, property title disputes are a recurring issue, and the legal status of transactions requires careful review by counsel before any engagement.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Nicosia

Courts sitting in Nicosia

Since the court reform of 1 July 2023, Cyprus has a three-tier system: District Courts at first instance, the Court of Appeal, and the Supreme Constitutional Court, with a separate Supreme Court. The Nicosia District Court hears civil and commercial claims for the capital district, and the appellate courts sit in Nicosia. The iJustice e-filing system, launched in July 2021, covers most civil cases. The Civil Procedure Rules modelled on the English rules took effect on 1 September 2023.

Commercial and Admiralty Courts

Law 69(I)/2022 created a Commercial Court for disputes above 2 million euros, with exceptions, and an Admiralty Court, both able to use English where the interests of justice require. According to a practice guide updated in May 2026, neither had yet started operating, and admiralty claims were heard at first instance by a Supreme Court judge. Counsel should confirm current status, since commencement would change where Nicosia commercial disputes are heard.

Arbitration institutions

Cyprus has no dominant domestic arbitral institution, and parties to international contracts often choose the LCIA or ICC. In Nicosia, the Cyprus Chamber of Commerce and Industry administers arbitrations, normally under ICC rules, and the Cyprus Eurasia Dispute Resolution and Arbitration Centre is also based in the city. International commercial arbitration is governed by Law 101/1987, based on the UNCITRAL Model Law, and domestic arbitration by the Arbitration Law, Cap. 4.

Financial supervisors and corporate administration

The Central Bank of Cyprus and CySEC are based in Nicosia. CySEC oversees roughly 830 entities, including investment firms, fund managers and administrative service providers that act as directors, secretaries and nominees for Cypriot companies. Published CySEC decisions, settlements and registers are lawful research sources; supervisory files are confidential. The Registrar of Companies, described on the Cyprus country page, also operates from the capital.

The divided city

The UN-controlled buffer zone runs through the centre of Nicosia, and crossing points such as Ledra Street have been open to pedestrians since 2008. The northern part is administered by the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, recognised only by Turkey. Its registries, courts and land records are not part of the Republic's system, and the EU acquis is suspended there, so evidence and title from the north need separate legal assessment.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Nicosia

For matters touching Nicosia, TDSC first establishes where the relevant records and decisions actually sit: with the Registrar of Companies, a CySEC-supervised firm, a corporate service provider, a bank, or in the north outside the Republic's system. Desk research covers company filings, CySEC and Central Bank publications, Cypriot judgments, foreign registries and Greek-, English- and Turkish-language media, reviewed under the GDPR and Cypriot data protection law. Work for litigation is designed with Cypriot advocates who can seek court-ordered disclosure. Questions

Nicosia: Frequently Asked Questions

Can TDSC identify who is behind a Nicosia-administered company?

Often in part. Filed records show directors, secretaries and registered shareholders, but these are frequently nominees provided by a corporate service provider. TDSC combines filings with foreign registries, court records, financing documents and media to build an ownership picture, and identifies where only a court order or the client's own contractual rights could establish beneficial ownership conclusively.

Is the Nicosia Commercial Court operating?

Law 69(I)/2022 provides for a Commercial Court for disputes above 2 million euros and an Admiralty Court, but a practice guide updated in May 2026 reported that neither had begun operating. Commercial claims continue to be heard by the District Courts. Clients should ask Cypriot counsel to confirm the position when a dispute is filed.

Can TDSC obtain information from CySEC or the Central Bank?

No. TDSC uses what these regulators publish, such as registers of authorised firms, enforcement decisions, settlements and investor warnings. Supervisory correspondence and inspection files are confidential. Where a client needs non-public regulatory information, that is a matter for its counsel and the authority, through whatever formal route the law allows.

Can TDSC research a company in northern Nicosia?

TDSC can conduct lawful open-source and media research on businesses in the Turkish Cypriot-administered north. Records there are kept outside the Republic of Cyprus system and their legal status is contested, so TDSC flags the source of each record and recommends that counsel assess any transaction, property title or judgment before the client relies on it.

Does TDSC have staff in Nicosia?

No. TDSC has no office, staff or address in Cyprus. Engagements are scoped and managed from Nashville. Where a matter requires document retrieval, court attendance or discreet local inquiries in Nicosia, TDSC coordinates independent qualified professionals and works alongside the client's Cypriot advocates, within a written scope agreed before work starts.
